title: Track-level Features
text:
This section examines Spotify’s track-level audio features to determine whether my favorite songs share consistent underlying characteristics, despite their diversity in genre, language, and artist.
The analysis focuses on six key features: danceability, energy, valence, tempo, loudness, and popularity. Together, these features capture how music feels rhythmically, emotionally, and physically.

The distributions show that most tracks fall within a relatively narrow range of danceability, with a strong concentration in the mid-to-high range. This suggests a consistent preference for rhythmically engaging music.

Core Relationship: Energy vs Valence



Energy vs Valence


This plot shows the relationship between energy and valence across all tracks.
While higher energy levels tend to correlate slightly with higher valence, the spread is wide. This indicates that tracks can be energetic without necessarily being emotionally positive.
This variation suggests that emotional tone is flexible within the playlist, while energy remains a more consistent driver of preference.

Spotify Features of My Favorite Tracks


This visualization combines multiple dimensions: danceability, energy, popularity, and genre.
Most tracks cluster within a similar region of mid-to-high danceability and moderate energy, regardless of genre or language. This reinforces the idea that personal preference is not primarily genre-driven, but instead centered around rhythmic and structural characteristics.
Outliers exist, but they reflect shifts in mood rather than entirely different listening preferences.

title: Track-level Features
text:
Key Findings
The playlist shows a clear pattern of consistency across several features.
Danceability is relatively high and tightly distributed, indicating a strong preference for rhythmically engaging tracks. Energy is also consistently moderate to high, reinforcing this pattern.
Valence shows more variation, suggesting that emotional tone is less important than rhythmic and structural qualities. Tempo varies more widely than expected, but still avoids extreme values.
Overall, the results indicate that personal music preference is not random, but driven by a consistent set of underlying audio characteristics — particularly rhythm and energy.
These patterns suggest that personal music preference is shaped more by consistent structural features than by genre or language.

The Playlist




The corpus is based on a personal Spotify playlist consisting of over 100 tracks.
Rather than being curated by genre or artist, the playlist reflects individual listening preferences — songs that stand out as favorites over time.

title: Background & Corpus
text:
The Corpus
The dataset consists of 102 tracks drawn from a personal Spotify playlist, representing individual listening preferences rather than a curated or genre-specific selection.
The playlist spans multiple languages (English, Dutch, and Spanish) and includes a wide range of genres such as rap, R&B, drill, pop, and soul. This diversity makes the dataset particularly suitable for investigating whether consistent patterns exist beneath apparent stylistic variation.
Although the playlist appears highly diverse, certain artists occur more frequently, including The Weeknd, Tory Lanez, Frenna, and Sevn Alias. This suggests that personal preference may already exhibit some degree of repetition at the artist level.
It is important to note that this corpus is not a random or representative sample of music. Tracks were selected based on personal preference, which introduces bias toward songs that are more memorable, emotionally engaging, or frequently played.
This makes the dataset especially relevant for exploring whether subjective taste can be explained through measurable audio features.

title: Background & Corpus
text:
Approach
This project applies computational analysis to identify patterns within a diverse personal music playlist.
The analysis focuses on Spotify audio features such as danceability, energy, valence, tempo, and loudness to determine whether consistent characteristics emerge across the dataset.
Feature distributions are examined to identify common ranges and tendencies, while relationships between variables are explored to detect underlying structure.
In addition, clustering techniques are used to investigate whether the playlist naturally groups into sub-patterns based on audio similarity, regardless of genre or artist.
The goal is to determine whether subjective listening preferences align with objective, data-driven patterns that are not immediately apparent through listening alone.

title: Background & Corpus
text:
Assumptions

Spotify audio features approximate perceptual musical qualities

Personal listening preferences reflect underlying patterns that can be quantified

Feature-based analysis provides deeper insight than genre labels alone

title: Chroma Features
text:
Chroma features describe how harmonic energy is distributed across the twelve pitch classes of Western music (C, C#, D, Eb, E, F, F#, G, Ab, A, Bb, B). Unlike raw frequency representations, chroma features are octave-invariant: they capture which notes are active, rather than how high or low they are.
This makes chroma particularly suitable for analysing harmonic structure, tonal centres, and repetition within a track.
For this analysis, The Weeknd – Wanderlust was selected as a representative track from the corpus.

title: Chroma Features
text:
Chromagram — Wanderlust



Chromagram – Wanderlust


The chromagram shows the intensity of each pitch class over time. Clear horizontal bands indicate pitch classes that remain active throughout the track, while vertical patterns reflect repetition of harmonic material.
In Wanderlust, several pitch classes are consistently active across the full duration of the track. Rather than a constantly shifting harmonic landscape, the track shows a stable distribution of pitch-class energy.

Interpretation
The repeated vertical structures indicate a loop-based harmonic organisation. The same harmonic material returns at regular intervals, which is typical for pop and R&B production.
At the same time, the presence of a limited number of dominant pitch classes suggests a stable tonal centre, rather than frequent modulation between keys.

title: Chroma Features
text:
Chord Activity — Wanderlust



Chordogram – Wanderlust


The chordogram compares the chroma features at each moment to a set of chord templates. Brighter regions indicate a stronger match between the audio signal and a given chord.
The visualisation shows that a small number of chords remain active throughout the track, with relatively little variation over time.

Interpretation
Rather than moving through a wide harmonic vocabulary, the track cycles through a limited set of chords. The lack of sharp transitions between different chord regions suggests that harmonic change is gradual and repetitive, rather than structurally complex.
This supports the idea that the harmonic structure is driven by repetition rather than progression.

title: Chroma Features
text:
Key Activity — Wanderlust



Keygram – Wanderlust


The keygram estimates the likelihood of different tonal centres over time by comparing chroma features to key templates.
The plot shows a clear dominance of a single key region across the track, with only minor variation in intensity.

Interpretation
The track remains centred around a stable tonal area, with little evidence of strong modulation. Although small fluctuations occur, they do not indicate structural key changes, but rather local variations in harmonic emphasis.
This reinforces the observation that the harmonic structure is consistent over time.

title: Chroma Features
text:
Key Findings
Across all visualisations, Wanderlust exhibits a clear pattern of harmonic stability and repetition:

The chromagram shows consistent activation of a limited set of pitch classes
The chordogram indicates a small and repeating chord vocabulary
The keygram confirms a stable tonal centre with minimal modulation

Together, these results suggest that the track relies on loop-based harmonic structures rather than harmonic complexity.

title: Chroma Features
text:
Connection to the Research Question
Although the playlist appears stylistically diverse, the chroma analysis suggests that this diversity does not necessarily extend to harmonic structure.
Instead, tracks may share underlying similarities in how harmony is organised:
through repetition, limited pitch-class usage, and stable tonal centres.
This supports the idea that a seemingly diverse playlist can still exhibit deep structural consistency.

title: Loudness & Energy
text:
Spotify’s loudness feature measures the overall intensity of a track in decibels (dB), where values closer to 0 indicate louder tracks. Unlike perceptual features such as energy, loudness reflects the actual acoustic level after mastering.
This section examines how loudness behaves across the corpus, and how it relates to other core features such as energy, acousticness, and danceability.

title: Loudness & Energy
text:
Loudness Distribution



Loudness Distribution


The distribution shows that most tracks fall within a relatively narrow loudness range, roughly between -10 dB and -5 dB.

Interpretation
This concentration suggests that loudness is not used as a highly expressive variable, but rather as a production standard. Tracks are mastered to similar levels, reflecting contemporary streaming and mastering practices where consistency in playback volume is prioritised.
A small number of quieter tracks (below -12 dB) appear as outliers, indicating occasional deviation from this norm.

title: Loudness & Energy
text:
Loudness vs Energy



Loudness vs Energy


There is a clear positive relationship between loudness and energy: louder tracks tend to have higher energy values.

Interpretation
Although energy is a perceptual measure and loudness is a physical one, they align strongly in this corpus. This suggests that perceived intensity is closely tied to mastering choices, with louder tracks generally being more compressed and dynamically dense.

title: Loudness & Energy
text:
Loudness vs Acousticness



Loudness vs Acousticness


A strong negative relationship is visible between loudness and acousticness. Tracks with high acousticness tend to be significantly quieter.

Interpretation
This reflects a clear divide between acoustic and produced sound. Acoustic tracks typically retain more dynamic range and are therefore quieter, while highly produced tracks are compressed and pushed to higher loudness levels.

title: Loudness & Energy
text:
Loudness vs Danceability



Loudness vs Danceability


The relationship between loudness and danceability is weaker, but still shows a slight positive trend.

Interpretation
Danceability is not directly driven by loudness, but louder tracks often coincide with more rhythmically stable and production-heavy structures, which can enhance perceived groove and movement.

title: Loudness & Energy
text:
Key Findings
Across all visualisations, loudness behaves as a controlled production parameter rather than a highly variable musical feature:

Loudness is tightly distributed, indicating consistent mastering practices

Louder tracks are generally more energetic

Acoustic tracks are systematically quieter

Loudness has a limited but positive relationship with danceability

title: Loudness & Energy
text:
Connection to the Research Question
While the playlist spans multiple genres and styles, loudness patterns reveal a shared production logic.
Rather than reflecting stylistic diversity, loudness remains relatively consistent across tracks. This supports the idea that the playlist exhibits underlying structural consistency in its sonic characteristics, even when surface-level features appear diverse.

Interpretation
The self-similarity matrix shows a largely continuous structure with only subtle block-like patterns. While the diagonal line confirms temporal progression, there are faint off-diagonal similarities indicating repeated sections, but without sharply defined boundaries.

title: Timbre Features
text:
What this means
Timbral variation in the track is relatively smooth and gradual. Instead of strong contrasts between sections, changes occur through shifts in texture, layering, and production density. This results in sections that are related rather than clearly separated, giving the track a cohesive sonic identity.

title: Timbre Features
text:
Connection to the research question
Despite stylistic diversity within the playlist, this suggests that timbral structure follows a consistent pattern of gradual evolution rather than abrupt change. Structural variation is therefore not primarily driven by timbre.

title: Timbre Features
text:
Key Insight
The track exhibits timbral continuity with limited contrast, reinforcing the idea that structure is shaped more by repetition and layering than by distinct changes in sound texture.
